R.N. c. Procureure générale du
Québec

2019 QCCS 6002

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

No:

500-17-102510-180

DATE:

JUNE 27, 2019

______________________________________________________________________

PRESIDED BY:

THE HONOURABLE

SILVANA CONTE, J.S.C.

______________________________________________________________________

R. N.

Plaintiff

v.

PROCUREURE GÉNÉRALE DU
QUÉBEC

and

COMMISSION DES DROITS DE LA
PERSONNE

ET DES DROITS DE LAJEUNESSE

and

BOIES DRAPEAU BOURDEAU

and

ME MICHÈLE TURENNE

and

GERMAIN ROYER

and

CURATEUR PUBLIC DU QUÉBEC

and

ME GUY RÉGIMBAL

and

CIUSSS DU
NORD-DE-L’ÎLE-DE-MONTRÉAL

and

ANNE LAMONTAGNE

and

SOPHIE GOUIN

Defendants

______________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

______________________________________________________________________

[
1
]

Defendants seek the dismissal of Plaintiff’s Re-Amended
Introductory Motion in damages and abusive procedure dated May 27, 2019,
pursuant to articles 53 and 168 of the
Code of Civil Procedure
(“CCP”).

[
2
]

The Attorney General for Quebec (“AGQ”)
postponed its Motion to Dismiss
sine

die
as Plaintiff agreed to
modify the Re-Amended Introductory Motion in order to implead the AGQ as a
third party.

FACTS

[
3
]

Plaintiff is the daughter of the late M. H. (“M.
H.”) who lived with Plaintiff and Plaintiff’s partner until her removal from
her home on March 20, 2012. This action was brought further to complaints filed
by Plaintiff’s sister M... to the CLSC of St. Laurent now CIUSS du Nord-de-l’Île-de-Montréal
(“CIUSS”) on September 30, 2010.

[
4
]

In March and July 2009, M... brought M. H. to
the Jewish General Hospital complaining that M. H. was being financially
exploited by Plaintiff. However, the attending nurse and Dr. Zigman found that
there was no substance to the claim of abuse or dementia. Sibling rivalry was
noted in the file
[1]
.

[
5
]

On October 1, 2010, Defendant Anne Lamontagne,
who was assigned to M. H.’s CLSC file and M...’s complaint, accompanied M... to
Plaintiff’s home and completed an evaluation of M. H. expressing concern as to
her lack of adequate hygiene, medication for her blood pressure and general
isolation
[2]
.

[
6
]

On October 2, 2010, the follow up report by
another social worker concluded that there were no signs of neglect or abuse
[3]
.

[
7
]

On November 2, 2010, social worker Johanne
Salvanos concluded that M. H. suffered from mild dementia but denied that there
was any form of abuse
[4]
.

[
8
]

From October 2010 to June 2011, the police also
made visits to the Plaintiff’s home and advised Defendant Lamontagne that they
found no evidence of abuse and the file was closed at M. H.’s request
[5]
.

[
9
]

On June 10, 2011, M... filed a complaint with the
Commission des droits de la personne et des droits de la jeunesse (“CDP”) as to
financial and physical abuse of her mother by Plaintiff.

[
10
]

On August 25, 2011, the CDP proceeded with an
investigation and Defendant Germain Royer was mandated to investigate M...’s
complaint in order to ascertain whether there was sufficient evidence to file
proceedings against Plaintiff for exploitation.

[
11
]

The CDP and the CLSC made three visits to Plaintiff’s
home in February and March 2012 and noted that M. H.’s condition had not
improved.

[
12
]

On March 20, 2012, M. H. requested admittance to
the CHSLD Notre-Dame-de- la-Merci, now part of Defendant CIUSS.

[
13
]

On May 5, 2012, Defendant Lamontagne wrote in
her psychosocial report that M. H. sought refuge at the CHSLD and asked that
her daughter M... make all decisions concerning her person
[6]
. The CHSLD formally notified
the Public Curator.

[
14
]

On July 16, 2012, the Public Curator recommended
the establishment of a protective regime given that M... declined to take over M.
H.’s care, and declared M. H. permanently incapable to care for her person and
her property.

[
15
]

On September 17, 2012, the Superior Court
authorized M. H.’s placement in a home and rejected Plaintiff’s request for a
habeas
corpus
order.

[
16
]

On November 16, 2012, Plaintiff filed a
complaint against Defendants Lamontagne and Gouin alleging inaccuracies and
negligence in the drafting of the psychosocial report
[7]
.

[
17
]

On January 30, 2013, the CDP completed their
investigation and concluded that there were sufficient grounds to pursue
Plaintiff on the basis that M. H. was vulnerable and that there was evidence of
financial exploitation.

[
18
]

The CDP report was prepared by Mr. Royer and
translated for Plaintiff on March 5, 2013
[8]
.

[
19
]

On April 10 2013, Plaintiff sent her comments to
the CDP to complain about various inaccuracies contained in the report and the
violation of her Charter rights
[9]
.

[
20
]

On May 22, 2013, Plaintiff sent an addendum to
the CDP and complained of the errors and distortions in the social workers’
reports
[10]
.

[
21
]

On September 11, 2013, the Superior Court granted
a request for treatment and placement of M. H. for a three year period.

[
22
]

In December 2013, the CDP filed a claim against
Plaintiff and the claim was amended in March 2015 seeking recovery of two
properties gifted to Plaintiff and hypothecated in the amount of $1,010,000
[11]
.

[
23
]

On September 24, 2014, the Superior Court
dismissed Plaintiff’s request to homologate a mandate of incapacity and granted
the Public Curator’s request to open a protection regime. The Public Curator was
named to administer M. H.’s person and property after finding that it was not
in M. H.’s best interests to be placed in Plaintiff’s care
[12]
.

[
24
]

On March 17, 2015, the Court of Appeal
maintained the Superior Court judgment concerning the protective regime
[13]
.

[
25
]

In March 2015, the CDP trial commenced before
the Human Rights Tribunal and continued sporadically over a period of 13 days
until January 22, 2016
[14]
.
The Public Curator was impleaded as an interested party but did not present any
evidence.

[
26
]

On November 10, 2016, Judge Hughes dismissed the
CDP claim for financial, physical and emotional exploitation finding that the
CDP had not met its burden. More importantly, he concluded that the CDP
investigation contained various irregularities and deficiencies and, in
conjunction with Defendant Lamontagne’s reports, showed a lack of objectivity
and zealousness
[15]
.
However, Judge Hughes did not award costs to Plaintiff as he found Plaintiff’s
conduct to be dilatory and abusive and stated that her explanations regarding
the donation were not credible
[16]
.

[
27
]

On June 5, 2018, Plaintiff filed the present
lawsuit seeking moral damages in the amount of $1.5 million and punitive
damages in the amount of $800,000 for the intentional interference of her
rights.

[
28
]

Plaintiff holds all persons involved in the removal
of her mother M. H. from her home, on March 20, 2010, responsible for her
damages, namely: the CIUSS, the Public Curator, the CDP, as social workers Defendants
Lamontagne and Gouin, investigator Defendant Germain Royer, and attorneys for
the CDP and the Public Curator respectively, Me Turenne and Me Régimbal.

[
29
]

At the hearing, Plaintiff confirmed that, despite
the lengthy historical narrative in her claim, the cause of action is based solely
on the abusive proceedings filed against her by the CDP in March 2015 before
the Human Rights Tribunal and the participation of all Defendants therein.

THE
APPLICABLE LAW

[
30
]

The Supreme Court of Canada has held that judges
must be cautious not to dismiss an action on a preliM. H.ry exception unless it
is “plain and obvious that it lacks a basis in law”
[17]
.

[
31
]

The Court of Appeal has summarized the
applicable principles as follows
[18]
:

•

The facts alleged in the action are deemed to be
true as well as, the exhibits filed in support thereof, however, not the legal characterization
of these facts;

•

Only the trial judge seized of the merits of the
case can determine whether the Plaintiff has met his burden of proof. If there
is a chance that Plaintiff’s allegations could eventually give rise to the
conclusions sought, then the Court must allow the action to continue;

•

the preliM. H.ry exception must be decided regardless
of the complexity of the questions of law; and

•

In case of doubt, the Court must exercise
caution and allow the case to proceed rather than prematurely dismissing the
action.

[
32
]

Defendants rely on prescription as the principal
ground for dismissal. Articles 2925 and 2926 CCQ provide that an action to
enforce personal rights are prescribed by three years and that the starting
point runs from the day the injury appears for the first time
[19]
.

[
33
]

In light of these principles, the Court will
examine each of the Defendants’ Applications to dismiss.

ANALYSIS

Defendants CIUSS,
Anne Lamontagne and Sophie Gouin

[
34
]

Plaintiff seeks to hold Defendants CIUSS,
Lamontagne and Gouin responsible for their evaluations of M. H. and her removal
from Plaintiff’s home on March 20, 2012. She further blames them for repeating
the contents of said evaluations before the Human Rights Tribunal.

[
35
]

The social workers’ involvement in the removal
of M. H. from Plaintiff’s home dates back to October 2010
[20]
with their first intervention
and evaluation. Their involvement continued until M. H. was assessed as being
totally and permanently incapable of caring for her person and her property and
was removed from Plaintiff’s home on March 20, 2012
[21]
.

[
36
]

Plaintiff had sufficient knowledge of the facts
required to institute a lawsuit against Defendant, as early as March 20, 2012
when M. H. was removed from Plaintiff’s home and as late as November 16, 2012
[22]
, when Plaintiff filed a
complaint against Defendants Lamontagne and Gouin concerning the social
workers’ evaluations alleging the same inconsistencies, faults and
Charter

violations as described in the Re-Amended Introductory Motion.

[
37
]

Therefore, Plaintiff’s action against these
Defendants was prescribed at the latest on November 16, 2015.

[
38
]

Plaintiff only instituted proceedings against
Defendants CIUSS, Lamontagne and Gouin on June 5, 2018.

[
39
]

Plaintiff argues that the medical files
concerning M. H. were not provided to her on January 22, 2014 and that she only
understood the information at the hearing before Judge Hughes in 2015 and upon
receipt of his judgment on November 10, 2016
[23]
.

[
40
]

This argument is not retained by the Court.

[
41
]

Even assuming that additional medical records
were only provided to Plaintiff on January 22, 2014. Plaintiff’s claim is still
prescribed as she had sufficient knowledge of the alleged fault to institute
the action, before receipt of the medical files in January 2014
[24]
.

[
42
]

Moreover, even if the medical records were
required to institute a claim, Plaintiff and her counsel were present at the 2014
hearing for the opening of the protection regime for M. H. where Defendants’
2012 reports and the medical records were filed and discussed and did not
institute an action within the three year prescription period
[25]
.

[
43
]

As for the abuse of proceedings claim,
Defendants were not parties to the CDP hearing before the Human Rights Tribunal
and cannot be responsible for the CDP decision, investigation or lawsuit
against Plaintiff. This cause of action is manifestly unfounded and frivolous
within the meaning of article 51 CPC.

[
44
]

Therefore, for all of these reasons, the action
instituted against Defendants CIUSS, Lamontagne and Gouin is dismissed.

Public
Curator

[
45
]

Plaintiff holds the Public Curator responsible
for seeking the opening of a protective regime for M. H. on the basis of false
evidence as well as, participating in the alleged abusive proceedings filed by
the CDP before the Human Rights Tribunal.

[
46
]

The claim against the Public Curator for the
opening of a protective regime is clearly prescribed.

[
47
]

The Public Curator was named curator to M. H.’s
person and property on September 24, 2014
[26]

after seeking the opening of a protective regime as early as August 16, 2012. Moreover,
all information relied upon by the Public Curator was disclosed to Plaintiff
and her attorney before and during the hearing before the Superior Court which
ended on June 3, 2014.

[
48
]

The action filed is also manifestly ill-founded within
the meaning of article 51 CCP.

[
49
]

First, Plaintiff seeks to indirectly appeal the final
judgment rendered by the Court on September 24, 2014 and later maintained on
appeal, which granted the Public Curator’s application for the opening of a
protective regime.

[
50
]

Second, the Public Curator did not bring the
alleged abusive proceedings against Plaintiff and cannot be held responsible
for the actions and conduct of the trial by the CDP. In addition, the Public
Curator was simply a third party acting on behalf of M. H.’s interests and did
not bring evidence or intervene other than to make oral representations on her
behalf.

[
51
]

For all of these reasons, the action instituted against
the Public Curator is dismissed.

Me Guy Régimbal

[
52
]

Me Régimbal acted as the attorney for the Public
Curator who was appointed to act for M. H.’s person and property.

[
53
]

Plaintiff holds Me Régimbal responsible for the
following faults:

53.1.

The abusive proceedings filed by the CDP before
the Human Rights Tribunal
[27]
;

53.2.

The fact that he failed to convince the CDP to
abandon the case or properly evaluate the credibility of witnesses at the
hearing
[28]
;

53.3.

Did not act as a prudent and diligent officer of
the Court in promoting her interests; acted in bad faith and violated her
Charter rights
[29]
.

[
54
]

The allegations of fault are manifestly
unfounded on its face. Me Régimbal did not represent the CDP. He cannot be held
responsible for the decision of the CDP to file a claim against Plaintiff before
the Human Rights Tribunal nor the CDP’s decision to pursue that claim where the
evidence was deemed to be insufficient by the Human Rights Tribunal.

[
55
]

Moreover, contrary to Plaintiff’s allegations, Me
Régimbal had no duty to represent or promote Plaintiff’s interests as an
officer of the Court. His decision to align himself with the CDP was one that
was fully within his mandate to act on behalf of M. H.’s interests.

[
56
]

At the hearing, Plaintiff stated that defamation
was not a cause of action being invoked in support of her claim. However, it
should be noted that such a cause of action would have been prescribed in any
event as the lawsuit was filed more than one year after the oral argument ended
before the Human Rights Tribunal on January 22, 2013
[30]
.

[
57
]

Finally, Me Régimbal benefits from relative
immunity from civil liability while acting in his role as attorney for the
Public Curator
[31]
.
The general allegations concerning Me Régimbal’s alleged bad faith are vague
and insufficient to support a
prima facie
claim for fault. These
allegations consist solely of Plaintiff’s legal characterizations of his
conduct which are not deemed to be true.

[
58
]

Therefore, the action against Me Régimbal is
dismissed.

The CDP,
Germain Royer and Me Michel Turenne

[
59
]

The CDP was created under
section 57
of the
Charter
of Human Rights and Freedoms
[32]
.

It

investigated and pursued the complaint filed alleged against
Plaintiff regarding the possible exploitation of M. H. under
section 48
of the
Charter
.

[
60
]

Mr. Royer was the investigator working on the
complaint and Me Turenne acted as the attorney for the CDP before the Human
Rights Tribunal.

[
61
]

The CDP and its employees benefit from immunity
from civil liability under
section 68
of the
Charter
.
Section 68
provides
the CDP and its investigators with absolute immunity with regard to its powers
of investigation, which are those provided under section 16 of an
Act Respecting
Public Inquiry Commissions
[33]
.

[
62
]

This section also provides its employees with
relative immunity in the exercise of their functions.

[
63
]

There are limited exceptions that can be invoked
to override the protection afforded by the
Charter
. As such, Plaintiff
will have to establish a
prima facie
case that the CDP, its investigator
or its employees knowingly and in bad faith acted outside their jurisdiction
[34]
.

Germain Royer

[
64
]

In the case of Mr. Royer, he benefits from
absolute immunity. Plaintiff claims that: he did not properly conduct his
investigation into the complaint of exploitation; his investigation was “botched”
and biased and his report misleading
[35]
.

[
65
]

Assuming the allegations of negligence are true,
the action instituted against Mr. Royer on June 5, 2018 is prescribed
[36]
.

[
66
]

The facts which form the basis of Plaintiff’s
claim against Mr. Royer were known to Plaintiff as late as April 10, 2013, as
appears from her letter commenting on the alleged errors in his investigation
report which was translated for Plaintiff on March 5, 2013
[37]
.

[
67
]

Moreover, as Mr. Royer benefits from absolute
immunity from civil liability, the vague allegations concerning his alleged bad
faith are insufficient grounds to invoke the exception to immunity. Moreover,
these allegations are legal characterizations of the facts by Plaintiff which
are not deemed to be true.

[
68
]

Therefore, for all of these reasons the action
filed against Mr. Royer is dismissed.

Me Michel
Turenne

[
69
]

Plaintiff holds Me Turenne responsible for the alleged
abusive of proceedings filed by the CDP.

[
70
]

As attorney for the CDP, Me Turenne benefits
from relative immunity from civil liability. He also benefits from the immunity
granted to employees of the CDP pursuant to
section 68
of the
Charter
.

[
71
]

There are no factual allegations to support Plaintiff’s
legal characterization of bad faith or abuse by Me Turenne in the conduct of
the CDP proceedings before the Human Rights Tribunal.

[
72
]

The decisions to call certain witnesses, make
objections or file evidence deemed necessary to pursue the claim are not
examples of bad faith but rather the normal decision making process for
litigation attorneys acting within the confines of their mandate.

[
73
]

On its face, the action filed against Me Turenne
is manifestly unfounded and is dismissed.

CDP

[
74
]

The CDP benefits from absolute immunity from civil
liability under
section 68
of the
Charter
.

[
75
]

The Plaintiff holds the CDP responsible for
bringing an abusive claim against Plaintiff and generally for the conduct of
its employees.

[
76
]

As the Court has dismissed the claims against
the employees, as either prescribed or ill-founded, the sole issue to be
determined is whether the allegations concerning the actions of the CDP meet
the stringent exception to absolute immunity from civil liability.

[
77
]

Plaintiff’s entire case is based upon the
premise that the CDP was wrong to pursue her for exploitation and to continue
the suit in face of insufficient evidence. There are numerous allegations in
the Re-Amended Introductory Motion of stress and the unfairness of the
allegations brought against Plaintiff which eventually were dismissed.

[
78
]

Nevertheless, while the Human Rights Tribunal
dismissed the CDP claim for lack of evidence and some procedural irregularities,
it did not find that there was an abuse of proceedings. In fact, the claim
against Plaintiff was dismissed but the Tribunal did not award costs to
Plaintiff on the basis of her own abusive conduct
[38]
.

[
79
]

The CDP is protected by absolute immunity from
civil liability and there are no factual allegations to support an argument
that it acted outside its jurisdiction or brought the claim in bad faith. The
allegations to that effect consist of Plaintiff’s legal characterization of the
facts which are not deemed to be true and which are insufficient to support a
claim for abusive proceedings on a
prima facie
basis.

[
80
]

Therefore, the Court concludes that the action
filed against the CDP is manifestly unfounded and has no chance of success.
Therefore the claim against the CDP is dismissed.

FOR THESE
REASONS, THE COURT:

[
81
]

GRANTS

Defendants’ applications to dismiss Plaintiff’s Re-Amended Introductory Motion;

[
82
]

THE WHOLE
with
legal costs.
